method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)' (published 27 August 2025), 21 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12608058). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline' (published 1 September 2021), 10 claims; LICENCE: © 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine (no open licence; PMC not open access) (read at PMC article page (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351) copyright and licence information). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the AASM 2021 GRADE-based clinical practice guideline, read from the PMC article page (tables stripped). S1 claims are unchanged. The EAN/ESRS/EU-NN 2021 European guideline (Bassetti et al., CC BY-NC-ND) was sought first: the Wiley publisher PDF and every open repository copy listed by Unpaywall and OpenAlex (HAL Montpellier, Unimore IRIS, Leiden, Helsinki, University of Copenhagen, Bern) returned bot challenges or access blocks, which were not bypassed. Europe PMC search: narcolepsy AND guideline/consensus/recommendations 2019-2026.

claims.claim: **Narcolepsy is a central hypersomnolence disorder.** Its core is excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), accompanied to a variable degree by cataplexy, hallucinations on falling asleep or waking, sleep paralysis and broken night sleep.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Onset has two peaks:** one in adolescence and a second in the third decade; a small number are diagnosed as children.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **In a patient with EDS, cataplexy is pathognomonic of narcolepsy type one (NT1):** a sudden loss of voluntary muscle tone while the person stays fully conscious.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Screen for common comorbidities:** depression, anxiety and ADHD lead the list, then metabolic problems (overweight, obesity, diabetes) and other sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), restless legs and REM sleep behaviour disorder.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep the differential for sleepiness wide:** insufficient sleep, circadian rhythm disorders and shift work, OSA and psychiatric illness can each mimic narcolepsy or coexist with it.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnosis is often late, and sometimes wrong.** The median delay from first symptoms is 6.0 to 10.5 years, yet in one UK series half of those referred as narcolepsy did not have it on formal assessment.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **ICSD-3-TR criteria:** ongoing EDS plus either a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) that meets the diagnostic threshold, or a qualifying CSF orexin level. An MSLT is an overnight polysomnogram followed by, usually, five daytime nap opportunities.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Separate NT1 from NT2:** NT1 needs cataplexy or a low CSF orexin. The distinction matters because NT1 is lifelong, while narcolepsy without cataplexy can remit.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Clear cataplexy plus a sleep-onset REM period on the overnight study is now enough for NT1**, without also needing a mean MSLT sleep latency of 8 min or less.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **An MSLT cannot diagnose on its own.** Rule out other causes of short sleep latency first (sleep deprivation, medicines, shift work), and remember antidepressants can suppress REM and hide sleep-onset REM periods.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **CSF orexin testing is available to Australians but hard to get:** it needs a lumbar puncture, the sample goes overseas through selected pathology companies, and Medicare does not cover it, so the patient pays.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **HLA typing is not a diagnostic criterion.** Its negative predictive value for NT1 exceeds 99%, so a negative result can argue against NT1 when the picture is atypical.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Non-drug measures support drug treatment:** a regular sleep schedule with planned short daytime naps for sleepiness, plus psychological support where needed, regular exercise and a balanced diet.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Match the drug to the symptom profile, comorbidities and patient preference.** Many narcolepsy drugs can be misused and are tightly regulated.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Australia differs on first-line drug for sleepiness.** European and AASM guidance prefers modafinil (with strong evidence also for pitolisant and solriamfetol, neither available here). Australian guidance lists modafinil or armodafinil, with dexamfetamine second; but the PBS requires a contraindication to dexamfetamine before it subsidises modafinil or armodafinil, making dexamfetamine the effective first subsidised option.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In New Zealand**, modafinil, dexamfetamine and methylphenidate are funded for narcolepsy through Pharmac Special Authority. Lisdexamfetamine may help, but both countries fund it only for ADHD.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Cataplexy:** sodium oxybate is the international first choice, but it is not on the PBS or the ARTG and is costly via the Special Access Scheme (Western Australia's state formulary is the exception). Antidepressants are used against cataplexy; clomipramine is the only one the PBS lists for it.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **AASM strong recommendations for adults with narcolepsy of either type:** modafinil, pitolisant, sodium oxybate and solriamfetol. **Conditional:** armodafinil, dexamfetamine (dextroamphetamine) and methylphenidate. Each was judged against no treatment, and the order is alphabetical within strength, not a ranking.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **What each drug improved in trials:** cataplexy responded to pitolisant, sodium oxybate and dexamfetamine; modafinil and solriamfetol improved sleepiness and disease severity (modafinil also quality of life).
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Certainty of evidence:** high for solriamfetol; moderate for modafinil, pitolisant, sodium oxybate and armodafinil; very low for dexamfetamine and methylphenidate.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Not enough evidence to recommend either way** in adult narcolepsy: scheduled naps, SSRIs and SNRIs, l-carnitine, selegiline and triazolam. Being left off the list is not advice against a treatment.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Tailor and review the choice** by age, pregnancy status and plans, comorbidity (including cardiovascular disease), allergy or past adverse reactions, misuse risk and treatment goals, and reassess at follow-up as life changes. Whatever the drug, many patients also need work or study accommodations, sleep hygiene and CBT or psychological support.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Closely related compounds** (modafinil and armodafinil; dexamfetamine, mixed amphetamine salts and lisdexamfetamine) may reasonably be assumed to carry similar benefits and risks, although the AASM graded single drugs rather than classes.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Common adverse effects:** modafinil, headache, insomnia, nausea, diarrhoea and dry mouth; pitolisant, headache, weight gain, insomnia and nausea (none led to stopping); sodium oxybate, nausea, headache, dizziness, bedwetting, chest discomfort, disturbed sleep and sleep-disordered breathing; solriamfetol, headache, nausea, insomnia, reduced appetite and chest discomfort, mostly mild or moderate.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Sodium oxybate** has an FDA boxed warning as a central nervous system depressant that can depress breathing; it is the sodium salt of GHB, whose misuse, especially with alcohol or sedating drugs, can cause seizures, coma and death. **Dexamfetamine and methylphenidate** are Schedule II drugs with boxed warnings about misuse and dependence.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Plan for pregnancy.** European guidance strongly advises stopping narcolepsy drugs before conception, accepting that symptoms will worsen, or using a single drug if stopping is not practical. Modafinil and armodafinil carry higher rates of congenital anomalies and make the oral contraceptive pill less effective.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Dexamfetamine in pregnancy:** an Australian ADHD cohort found continued use was not linked to worse maternal or neonatal outcomes, though complications were somewhat lower in the unexposed group.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Counselling on pregnancy and contraception is often poor** and should be improved.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **AASM pregnancy remarks:** animal data suggest each drug may harm the fetus, and human data are too sparse to judge; the 2018 report of the US armodafinil/modafinil pregnancy registry showed more major congenital anomalies after exposure in the womb. Modafinil, armodafinil and pitolisant may weaken oral contraception. The AASM makes no specific recommendations for pregnancy or breastfeeding.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Children with narcolepsy (AASM, conditional):** modafinil or sodium oxybate. Modafinil lacks FDA approval under 17 years because of a boxed warning for Stevens–Johnson syndrome and psychosis from paediatric case reports. Sodium oxybate improved cataplexy, severity and sleepiness, but rare serious effects include central sleep apnoea, depression and suicidality. No eligible evidence was found for methylphenidate, amphetamines, scheduled naps or SSRIs/SNRIs for cataplexy in children.
claims.locator: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, task force (Maski K, Trotti LM, Kotagal S, Auger RR, Rowley JA, Hashmi SD, Watson NF), Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 17(9):1881–1893, doi 10.5664/jcsm.9328, 'Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline', published 1 September 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636351/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Orexin receptor (OX2R) agonists are the coming change.** Oveporexton has reduced sleepiness and cataplexy and improved wakefulness testing in NT1, with trials under way in Australia; an earlier agent was stopped for liver toxicity. Immunotherapy has little evidence and carries risk.
claims.locator: Lin, Yee, Tai, Sivam et al., Internal Medicine Journal (RACP) vol 55, doi 10.1111/imj.70186, 'Narcolepsy 2025 (with an Australasian perspective)', published 27 August 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12608058/, retrieved 2026-09-23
